case.label: A
case.text: A reader could argue that a security group rule limited to the VPC CIDR block already blocks the internet, and the load balancer sits inside the VPC, so the instances accept HTTP from the load balancer. This fails the stem in two ways: the instances keep public IP addresses in public subnets, so a network path from the internet still exists (the stem says to remove every path), and any other source inside the VPC could also reach the instances, but the stem says the load balancer and no other source. Option C (network ACL with load balancer IP addresses from a DNS lookup) is the next weakest rival; the addresses of a load balancer node change, and a network ACL is stateless, so it is brittle and not the most secure way. Option E fails because AWS WAF cannot be associated with an EC2 instance. No second defensible pair found.

case.label: A
case.text: Making the path / return HTTP 200 also makes the default health check pass, and a reader could say the 302 redirect is the bug introduced by the release, so fixing the application is the real fix. But it needs a new release to every instance, which is more operational work than editing one target group setting, and the stem asks for the LEAST operational overhead and for health checks that show the real state; the /health page exists for exactly that. Option D (TCP) would show healthy even if the application cannot serve requests, so it fails the real-state requirement. Wording cue: the stem describes /health in detail (returns 200 only when the application can serve), which points to C almost directly; this is a light giveaway but does not create a second answer.

case.label: D
case.text: Network Load Balancers now support security groups, so a reader who knows that feature could choose D because it is the smaller change and keeps the existing load balancer. It fails because the stem says the load balancer was created without security groups, and the AWS Network Load Balancer troubleshooting page says that a Network Load Balancer created without security groups cannot support security groups after creation (verified in the saved docs: elasticloadbalancing-network, 'Unable to associate a security group with a load balancer'). So D is not possible, and C (create a new load balancer with a security group and move clients) is the only option that meets the requirement. Option A leaves the 0.0.0.0/0 rule, so it does not limit the source to a load balancer. Option B states a false limit for new load balancers. Risk: a candidate who does not know the creation-time rule may defend D; the stem carries the needed constraint ('created years ago without security groups'), so this is not a missing constraint.

case.label: C
case.text: A Network Load Balancer with a TLS listener and a TLS target group encrypts both hops, so a reader who focuses on 'protect the data in transit on every network hop' could pick it. It fails the explicit requirement that the TLS session the client opens must end on an instance: with a TLS listener the session ends on the load balancer (it decrypts with the ACM certificate) and a second, separate session is opened to the target. Options A and D also terminate the client session at the Application Load Balancer, and D sends plain HTTP to the instances. Only the TCP listener passes the client's TLS session through to the instance. Wording cue: 'decrypts the traffic with its own certificate and private key' and 'hold certificates' in every option are strong hints toward pass-through, but all four options mention certificates, so the cue does not single out B by itself.
